s: Pelias is oppressed by old age and becomes the target of Medea’s deception. His daughters, believing Medea can restore his youth, stab him while he sleeps, after which Medea cuts his throat and places him in the boiling cauldron.

l: daughters of Pelias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The daughters of Pelias believe Medea’s claim that old age can be removed after seeing her transform an aged ram into a lamb. At Medea’s urging, they stab their sleeping father, turning away their eyes because they cannot bear to see their own blows.

l: ram, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medea uses an aged ram to demonstrate her supposed power to restore youth. After she cuts it and places it with magical preparations in a cauldron, it emerges as a lamb, causing the daughters of Pelias to trust her.

l: old age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: rejuvenation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Rejuvenation is performed on Æson through Medea’s rites and magical mixture, causing his hoariness, leanness, paleness, and weakness to disappear. Medea falsely presents the transformation of the ram as proof that she can also rejuvenate Pelias.

l: Medea's enchantments, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medea’s magic includes invocations, sacrifices, herbs, enchanted waters, flames, sulphur, and a potion made from many strange ingredients. It restores Æson’s youth and creates the convincing transformation of an old ram into a lamb, enabling her deception of Pelias’s daughters.

l: revenge against Pelias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medea’s revenge against Pelias is carried out by feigning a quarrel with Jason and gaining the trust of Pelias’s daughters. She persuades them that they can restore their father’s youth, leading them to stab him and allowing her to complete his destruction.

l: death of Pelias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pelias’s daughters stab him while he sleeps, and he rises half-mangled and asks what they are doing. Before he can say more, Medea severs his throat and plunges his mangled body into the boiling cauldron, bringing about his death.

s: Medea may have administered a potion to Æson that supplied him with new spirits and strength. The text also suggests that she could have mixed venomous herbs into Pelias’s drink, producing his immediate death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

Ægeus celebrates Theseus’s survival with sacrifices and a public festival, while Minos prepares a war against Athens to avenge the death of his son Androgeus and gathers allied forces from several islands. s: Cerberus guards the gates of the Infernal Regions and has three heads. Hercules drags him away in chains; the dog barks furiously and scatters white foam over the fields.

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medea prepares aconite from the wolfsbane brought from Scythia and contrives for Ægeus to give it to Theseus. After Ægeus prevents Theseus from drinking it, Medea escapes by raising clouds through enchantments.

l: Ægeus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ægeus shelters Medea and marries her, though the text blames him for this deed. He unknowingly presents the poisoned cup to Theseus, then recognizes his son by the markings on his sword and knocks the cup away. Rejoicing that Theseus is safe, he offers sacrifices and gifts to the gods and celebrates with the people.

l: Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minos, king of Crete, prepares a war against Athens to avenge the death of his son Androgeus. He gathers auxiliary forces before the war and crosses the sea with a swift fleet, securing allies by treaty or conquest.

l: Androgeus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Androgeus is the son of Minos. He was murdered at Athens, and his death leads Minos to prepare a retaliatory war.

s: Androgeus’s death occurs at Athens, where he was murdered. Minos seeks to avenge it by preparing war against Athens and gathering auxiliary forces.

s: After Theseus survives Medea’s attempt, Ægeus holds a public celebration in his honor. Sacrifices are made, gifts are offered to the gods, and the senators and common people sing, drink, and praise Theseus’s heroic deeds.

s: Athens sends Cephalus to request military assistance from Æacus against the effort to subdue all Achaia. Æacus agrees to provide the forces of his kingdom.

l: lands (Æacus's lands), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

s: Themis sends the wild beast against Aonian Thebes after the son of Laius solves the riddle of the mysterious propounder. It ravages cattle and people, evades the hunters and their nets, and is finally transformed into a marble statue while being pursued by Lælaps.

l: javelin, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The javelin is a beautiful weapon of unknown wood with a golden point, given to Procris by Cynthia and later given by Procris to Cephalus. Whatever it is aimed at, it strikes, does not depend on chance, and returns stained with blood without anyone retrieving it.

s: Erectheus united Cephalus and Procris, and their love and recent marriage initially made Cephalus happy. Their marriage is threatened by Cephalus’s suspicion and deceptive test, but after he confesses his fault and asks forgiveness, they are restored to one another and live harmoniously.

s: Cephalus returns to Athens disguised and offers Procris increasingly large sums for one night, hoping to discover whether she has been faithful. She resists his advances and says she is reserved for her husband, but he finally reveals himself and accuses her, causing her to flee in shame.

s: Neighboring youths surround the extensive fields with nets to hunt the wild beast sent against Thebes, but it leaps over the nets and barriers. Lælaps is released and pursues it in circles across the plain, while Cephalus watches from a hill and prepares his javelin.

s: As Lælaps and the wild beast remain evenly matched in speed, Cephalus looks away while preparing to throw his javelin. When he looks back, both have become marble statues standing in the middle of the plain, apparently frozen in their contest.

s: Procris became jealous after hearing that Cephalus repeatedly called upon the breeze in affectionate words, believing that he loved a Nymph. s: Cephalus describes his early marriage with Procris as mutually loving and happy, and he says that no other woman could have captivated him. He later mistook the sound of Procris concealed in the thicket for a wild beast and killed her with his javelin.

l: Nymph Aura, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Nymph Aura was imagined by Procris to be Cephalus’s beloved rival. Cephalus explains that the name referred only to the breeze, not to an actual Nymph.

s: The javelin had previously been given to Cephalus by Procris. While hunting, Cephalus hurled it at what he thought was a wild beast, and it struck Procris in the breast.

s: Cephalus sought the breeze as a refreshing relief from the heat and his hunting exertions. He addressed it with words of affection, and those ambiguous words led Procris to believe that he loved another.

s: Cephalus and Procris’s marriage was initially marked by mutual kindness, social love, and equal affection. As she was dying, Procris invoked their marriage ties while asking Cephalus not to share them with the supposed Nymph Aura.

s: Procris's death resulted from Cephalus’s mistaken belief that the noise she made while concealed in the thicket came from a wild beast. Before dying, she learned that Aura was only the breeze and appeared more contented and free from care.

s: Procris received the wound in the middle of her breast from the javelin. Cephalus lifted her body, tried to bind and staunch the cruel wound, and begged her not to die.

s: Alcathoë is the city ruled by Nisus and is attacked by Minos. Its fortunes in the war remain uncertain until Scylla cuts off the lock that safeguards the kingdom.

s: Nisus rules Alcathoë, and a purple lock among his hoary hairs protects his kingdom. After Scylla cuts off the lock, Nisus is transformed into a sea eagle and pursues her with his crooked beak.

s: The purple lock of Nisus is the safeguard of his powerful kingdom. Scylla cuts it off while he sleeps and gives it to Minos as the price of her love and her country's surrender.

s: Scylla, the daughter of Nisus, falls passionately in love with Minos and betrays her father and country by cutting off Nisus's purple lock. Minos rejects her, and she follows his departing fleet before being transformed into Ciris.

l: war between Minos and Nisus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE EIGHTH.
s: The war begins with Minos's attack on the coasts and city ruled by Nisus. Its outcome remains in suspense for a long time, until Scylla's removal of the purple lock enables Minos to prevail.

l: love of Scylla for Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE EIGHTH.
s: Scylla's love for Minos grows as she watches him fight, and she wishes to surrender her city and herself to him. She believes that giving him the purple lock will end the war and secure his love, but Minos does not return her passion.

s: Scylla's treachery consists of entering her father's chamber and cutting off the lock that protects his kingdom. She delivers the lock to Minos, who condemns her as a disgrace and refuses to reward the crime.

l: siege of Alcathoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE EIGHTH.
s: During the siege of Alcathoë, Minos and Nisus remain opposed while victory shifts uncertainly between them. The siege ends when Scylla removes the purple lock and Minos gains control of the city.

s: Crete is the realm of Minos and the birthplace of Jupiter. Minos refuses to allow Scylla, whom he considers a monster, to enter it.

s: When Scylla follows Minos's ships and Nisus, as a sea eagle, moves to tear her apart, she lets go of the stern. Feathers support her fall, and she is transformed into a bird called Ciris.

s: Ariadne helps Theseus find his way out of the Labyrinth by means of a thread. Theseus abandons her on Dia, where Bacchus embraces and aids her.

s: Dædalus, famed for his architectural skill, designs the Labyrinth for Minos. He fills it with innumerable winding passages and makes it so intricate that he can scarcely return to its entrance.

s: Bacchus embraces and aids Ariadne after Theseus abandons her. To give her lasting fame, he places her crown in the heavens as a constellation.

l: Labyrinth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: The Labyrinth is a dwelling of many divisions and confusing passages built by Dædalus to contain the Minotaur. Its intricate windings make escape difficult, but Theseus finds the entrance again with Ariadne’s help.

s: Ariadne’s thread enables Theseus to retrace his route through the Labyrinth and escape after killing the Minotaur. The explanation suggests that the thread may poetically represent a plan of the Labyrinth given to Ariadne or Theseus.

s: Bacchus takes the crown from Ariadne’s head and casts it into the air. Its jewels change into fires and settle into the shape of a crown in the heavens.

l: crown constellation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: The crown becomes a constellation to immortalize Ariadne’s name. It is placed between Hercules, represented as resting on his knee, and Ophiuchus, the figure holding serpents.

l: tribute to Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: The tribute consists of youths and virgins from the best Athenian families. According to the accounts cited, it is sent either each year or every nine years, with seven young men and seven virgins named by some authors.

l: Theseus's slaying of the Minotaur, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: Theseus kills the Minotaur after entering the Labyrinth and locating the difficult entrance again with Ariadne’s aid.

l: Theseus's abandonment of Ariadne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: After escaping the Labyrinth, Theseus carries Ariadne away but barbarously deserts her on Dia, which is identified with Naxos.

l: Ariadne's transformation of the crown, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: Ariadne’s crown is transformed into a constellation when Bacchus throws it into the yielding air and its jewels become fires while retaining the crown’s shape.

l: Crete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: Crete is ruled by Minos and contains his palace and the Labyrinth built by Dædalus. Theseus and the Athenian tribute travel there, and the Minotaur is confined there.

l: Naxos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, opening
s: Naxos, also called Dia, is the island where Theseus abandons Ariadne. There Bacchus finds, embraces, and aids her.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus, confined in Crete and longing for his native soil, constructs wings from feathers, thread, and wax so that he and his son Icarus can escape by air. Dædalus warns Icarus to fly between the sea and the Sun, but Icarus flies too high, causing the Sun to melt his wings and sending him to his death in the sea. Dædalus buries Icarus and later witnesses a partridge, which recalls the transformation of Perdix, his talented nephew whom he had thrown from a tower out of jealousy. Minerva saves Perdix by transforming him into a partridge, a bird that thereafter avoids high places.

l: Dædalus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus, weary of his exile in Crete and longing for his native soil, devises wings to escape by air. He constructs the wings from feathers, thread, and wax, flies ahead of Icarus, and repeatedly looks back to guide and protect him. After Icarus dies, Dædalus buries him and curses his own arts; the explanation identifies Dædalus as a talented Athenian famed for statuary and architecture who had killed his nephew out of jealousy.

l: Icarus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Icarus assists Dædalus while the wings are being made, playfully handling the feathers and softening the wax. Although Dædalus warns him to keep to the middle course, Icarus becomes exhilarated by a bolder flight, abandons his guide, and rises toward the Sun.

l: Perdix (Talos), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Perdix, also called Talos in the explanation, is Dædalus's nephew, a boy eager to learn. He invents the saw by imitating the backbone of a fish and makes a compass from two arms of iron, but Dædalus, jealous of his talent, throws him from the sacred citadel of Minerva.

l: Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Minos controls the land and sea around Crete, but Dædalus observes that he cannot control the air. The explanation says that Minos kept Dædalus in prison after learning that he had assisted Pasiphaë, and that Dædalus escaped by ship.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Minerva supports Perdix during his fall and transforms him into a bird. She is described as favoring ingenuity.

l: Crete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Crete is the place where Dædalus is held in prolonged exile and from which he seeks to escape. Dædalus considers the island and surrounding sea controlled by Minos, while the sky remains open to him.

l: Icaria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Icaria is the name later given to the sea or island associated with Icarus's fall. The footnote explains that the island of Samos, being near the place where he fell, received the name Icaria.

l: the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: The Sun's heat softens and melts the fragrant wax fastening Icarus's wings when he flies too high.

l: Dædalus's wings, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus makes wings by arranging feathers from shortest to longest, binding them with thread and wax, and bending them to imitate bird wings. He fits them to his and Icarus's shoulders, and they use them to fly from Crete.

l: wax (Dædalus's wings), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Wax binds the feathers in Dædalus's wings and is softened by Icarus while the wings are being made. The Sun later melts the wax, leaving Icarus without functioning wings.

l: partridge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: A newly made partridge watches Dædalus bury Icarus and expresses delight through its calls. The bird retains the vigor of Perdix's former genius, flies near the ground, nests in hedges, and avoids high places because it remembers its fall.

l: Dædalus's exile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus's prolonged exile in Crete makes him abhor the island and long for his native soil. The footnote says his exile followed the killing of one of his scholars in a fit of jealousy, probably Perdix.

l: escape from Crete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus escapes from Crete by constructing wings and traveling through the air with Icarus. The explanation presents the wings as a poetic version of his escape by ship, using sails to evade Minos's oared vessels.

l: flight of Dædalus and Icarus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: Dædalus flies ahead of Icarus, instructing him to remain between the sea and the Sun and warning him against certain constellations. They pass islands including Samos, Delos, Paros, Lebynthus, and Calymne before Icarus leaves Dædalus's guidance and climbs higher.

l: Icarus's fall and death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: When the Sun melts the wax of Icarus's wings, he shakes his bare arms and can no longer catch the air. He falls into the sea while calling for Dædalus, and Dædalus later buries his body; the sea and nearby land are associated with his name.

l: transformation of Perdix, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [VIII.183-259]
s: After Dædalus throws Perdix from the citadel of Minerva, Minerva receives him in midair and transforms him into a partridge. As a bird, he retains his former name and ingenuity but avoids lofty regions because he remembers his fall.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Diana punishes Œneus and Calydon because he omits her from his offerings by sending a monstrous boar to ravage the land. Meleager leads a company of heroes, including Theseus and Atalanta, in the Calydonian boar hunt and kills the beast after Atalanta wounds it. When the sons of Thestius seize the boar’s head and hide from Atalanta, Meleager kills Plexippus and Toxeus. Althæa then burns the fatal billet linked to Meleager’s life, causing his death, after which Diana transforms most of his mourning sisters into birds.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Diana is angered because Œneus omits her from his offerings and sends a monstrous boar to ravage Calydon in revenge. After Meleager’s death, she is said to transform most of his sisters into birds.

l: Œneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Œneus offers first fruits to Ceres, Bacchus, and Minerva and continues the honors to the other Gods, but omits Diana. His lands are consequently ravaged by the boar, and he later mourns Meleager’s death.

l: Calydon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Calydon is ravaged by Diana’s boar, which destroys crops, vines, olive branches, and livestock until Meleager and the assembled heroes confront it. After Meleager dies, Calydon lies prostrate in mourning.

l: Theseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Theseus is celebrated for ending Athens’s mournful tribute, and his fame spreads throughout the Argive cities and Achaia. He joins the Calydonian boar hunt with Pirithoüs and warns Pirithoüs not to attack the boar rashly after Ancæus is killed.

l: Meleager, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Meleager leads the Calydonian boar hunt and kills the boar after Atalanta wounds it. He gives the victory spoil to Atalanta and kills Plexippus and Toxeus when they take it from her. Althæa’s burning of the fatal billet causes Meleager to suffer a concealed burning death.

l: Atalanta, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Atalanta, the daughter of the king of Arcadia, joins the hunt armed with a bow. Her arrow first draws blood from the boar, and Meleager honors her by giving her the boar’s head and hide, provoking the envy of the others.

l: Calydonian boar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Diana sends the enormous boar to avenge her neglected worship. It devastates Calydon, kills or wounds several hunters, and is finally brought down after Atalanta wounds it and Meleager strikes it with his spear.

l: sons of Thestius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: The sons of Thestius participate in the hunt and object when Atalanta receives the boar’s head and hide. They seize the spoil from her, leading Meleager to kill them.

l: Plexippus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Plexippus, one of the sons of Thestius, helps take the boar’s spoil from Atalanta. Meleager pierces his breast with a sword.

l: Toxeus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Toxeus, Plexippus’s brother, hesitates between avenging his brother and avoiding the same fate. Meleager kills him with the weapon still reeking from Plexippus’s blood.

l: Ancæus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Ancæus boasts that men’s weapons are superior to women’s and attacks the boar with a battle-axe. The boar tears open his groin and kills him, and Meleager later regards Ancæus’s wounds as a happier death than his own.

l: Althæa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Althæa first rejoices in Meleager’s victory but turns to vengeance when she learns that he has killed her brothers, Plexippus and Toxeus. She struggles between her duties as mother and sister before throwing the fatal billet into the fire, and afterward takes her own life with a sword.

l: Fates, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: At Meleager’s birth, the three Fates place a billet in the flames and declare that the newborn and the wood will share the same span of life. Their pronouncement makes the billet’s survival essential to Meleager’s life.

l: fatal billet, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: The fatal billet is rescued from the fire at Meleager’s birth and hidden by Althæa, thereby preserving his life. When Althæa later throws it into the flames, it burns away and Meleager dies as it is consumed.

l: Meleager's sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Meleager’s sisters mourn him intensely, embracing and kissing his body and later grieving around his tomb. Diana transforms all except Gorge and the daughter-in-law of Alcmena into birds.

l: Calydonian boar chase, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: The hunt brings together Meleager, Theseus, Atalanta, and many other heroes against the boar sent by Diana. Several hunters are killed or wounded before Atalanta and Meleager help bring the animal down.

l: Meleager's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Meleager’s death results from Althæa’s decision to burn the billet whose life was joined to his. He feels his entrails scorched by hidden fire, laments that he dies without shedding blood, and gradually expires as the fire and his spirit are extinguished together.

l: transformation of Meleager's sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: Diana, finally satiated with the calamities of the house of Parthaon, gives wings to Meleager’s sisters, makes their mouths horny, and sends them through the air. Gorge and the daughter-in-law of Alcmena are excluded from the transformation.

l: boar's head and hide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [VIII.260-546]
s: After the boar is killed, Meleager presents its head and hide, still thick with stiff bristles and marked by huge tusks, to Atalanta as the spoil of victory. The sons of Thestius take the spoil from her, prompting Meleager’s attack on them.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: The unit explains the story of the Calydonian boar chase, focusing on Œneus, Diana, Meleager, and Althæa. Œneus was said to have offended Diana by forgetting her in his sacrifices, after which a wild boar ravaged his territory and killed country people. Meleager gathered neighboring nobles to destroy the boar, and the deaths of Plexippus and Toxeus led Althæa to condemn her son and to the invention of the fatal billet story. The explanation suggests that the legend may preserve historical events while the magical and metamorphic elements are poetic fiction.

l: Calydonian boar chase, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: The Calydonian boar chase is generally thought to be based partly on historical facts, though it contains much fabulous material. Meleager gathered neighboring nobles to destroy the boar after it ravaged Œneus’s dominions and killed country people.

l: Calydonian boar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: The Calydonian boar ravaged part of Œneus’s dominions, particularly a carefully cultivated vineyard, and killed some country people. The circumstances led people to say that Diana had sent it.

l: Meleager, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: Meleager collected the neighboring nobles to destroy the Calydonian boar. After Plexippus and Toxeus were killed, Althæa devoted him to the Furies; some writers say that she really poisoned him.

l: Althæa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: Althæa was the sister of Plexippus and Toxeus. In grief over their deaths, she devoted her son Meleager to the Furies and may have used magical incantations connected with the story of the fatal billet.

l: Œneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: Œneus offered the first fruits to the gods but forgot Diana in his sacrifices. A wild boar then ravaged part of his dominions, especially a vineyard on which he had spent much effort.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: Diana was said to have been offended because Œneus omitted her from his sacrifices. The boar that ravaged his territory was consequently said to have been sent by her.

l: Calydonian boar legend, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: The Calydonian boar legend is generally understood to combine historical facts with fabulous elements. Its account of the boar’s origin, Meleager’s death, the fatal billet, and the transformation of Meleager’s sisters is presented as poetic or legendary development.

l: fatal billet, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, [Footnote 23: _Cocalus._--Ver. 261. He was the king of Sicily, who
s: The fatal billet was part of the story explaining Meleager’s death. The explanation suggests that the story may have been invented after Althæa devoted her son to the Furies, perhaps with the aid of magical incantations.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Theseus is delayed by the swollen Acheloüs river and accepts Acheloüs's invitation to rest in his grotto. Acheloüs tells Theseus how five Naiads were swept into the sea and became the Echinades, and how Neptune transformed Perimele into an island after Acheloüs pleaded for her. Lelex then recounts how Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as men, were welcomed by Philemon and Baucis when their neighbors refused them lodging. The gods destroyed the surrounding village by flooding, changed the couple's cottage into a temple, granted their wish to serve there, and transformed them into adjoining trees; Acheloüs concludes by describing Proteus's ability to assume many shapes.

l: Theseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Returning from the chase of the Calydonian boar, Theseus is delayed by the swollen Acheloüs river. He accepts Acheloüs's invitation to rest in his grotto and listens to accounts of transformations performed by the gods.

l: Acheloüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Acheloüs, swollen with rain, warns Theseus about the danger of crossing the flooded river and receives him in his grotto. He recounts the transformations of the Naiads and Perimele, and later describes Proteus's many forms.

l: Acheloüs river flood, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: The flood delays Theseus and is described as strong enough to carry away beams, stones, folds, flocks, and people. In Acheloüs's account, a great flood also tears woods and fields from their places and carries the Naiads into the sea.

l: Lelex, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Lelex, a hero of Trœzen with grey hair, is present at Acheloüs's banquet. He defends the power of the gods and recounts how Jupiter and Mercury were received by Philemon and Baucis.

l: the Naiads, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Five Naiads hold a joyful festival after sacrificing twice five bullocks to the local gods, while neglecting Acheloüs. His rage and flood carry them into the sea, where the land is divided around them.

l: Echinades, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: The Echinades are five islands that appear in the sea where the Naiads were swept away. Acheloüs explains that his waves and those of the main divided the formerly continuous land into these parts.

l: Perimele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Perimele is a beloved Nymph whom Acheloüs says he deprived of her virginity. Her father, Hippodamas, pushed her from a rock into the sea, and Acheloüs sought Neptune's aid for her.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Neptune is invoked by Acheloüs as ruler of the flowing waters. He assents by moving his head, allowing Perimele to become a place in the sea.

l: transformation of Perimele into an island, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: As Perimele swims, her body grows hard and earth covers her breast and limbs. Fresh earth encloses her, and a heavy island grows from her transformed body.

l: island of Perimele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: The island of Perimele lies far from the other islands and is pleasing to Acheloüs. Mariners call it Perimele.

l: Philemon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Philemon, an old and poor man, lives with Baucis in their small cottage. He welcomes Jupiter and Mercury, helps prepare their meal, joins Baucis in requesting service in the gods' temple, and is transformed with her into a tree.

l: Baucis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Baucis, an old woman, receives Jupiter and Mercury hospitably when the surrounding houses refuse them. She prepares their meal, joins Philemon in requesting that they serve the gods, and becomes an adjoining tree with him.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Jupiter visits the home of Philemon and Baucis disguised as a man, together with Mercury. He reveals their divine identity, punishes the impious neighborhood, transforms the cottage into a temple, and grants the couple's request.

l: Mercury, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: Mercury accompanies Jupiter in human disguise after laying aside his wings and carrying the Caduceus. He is welcomed by Philemon and Baucis and participates in rewarding their hospitality and punishing the village.

l: village of Philemon and Baucis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]
s: The village contains many houses whose inhabitants refuse lodging to Jupiter and Mercury. Its inhabitants are punished when the village sinks into a morass, while the cottage of Philemon and Baucis remains.
